title: Tight Approximation Results for Matroid Optimization with a Linear Constraint
abstract:
We study the following class of matroid optimization problems with a linear constraint (𝒫-MOL). Given a matroid ℳ = (E,ℐ), two nonnegative weight functions v,w:E → ℝ_{≥ 0}, and a threshold L ∈ ℝ_{≥ 0}, find opt v(S) where S is either an independent set or a base of ℳ satisfying a budget-type constraint: w(S) ≤ L or w(S) ≥ L, and opt ∈ {min,max}. 𝒫-MOL provides a unified representation for a broad family of NP-hard optimization problems, including budgeted matroid independent set, constrained minimum-basis, and knapsack-cover variants with a matroid constraint. Also, it naturally extends to multiple matroid constraints. In particular, we consider the matroid intersection cover (MIC) problem, where feasibility is defined by the common independent sets of two matroids and one seeks minimum v(S) subject to w(S) ≥ L.
Our main result is a unified efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS) for all nontrivial 𝒫-MOL variants, obtained by generalizing a technique of Hassin and Levin (SIAM J. Comput., 2004) for solving the constrained minimum spanning tree problem. Specifically, for any fixed ε > 0, we present an algorithm running in time |E|^O(1) ⋅ (1/ε²)^O(1/ε) that outputs a feasible solution S whose value is at most (1+ε)OPT for minimization variants and at least (1-ε)OPT for maximization variants. This resolves the complexity status of all members of 𝒫-MOL, as none of these problems admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (Doron-Arad, Kulik and Shachnai, ICALP'24). Finally, we separate the 𝒫-MOL family from its extension to matroid intersection. We show that an EPTAS is unlikely to exist for the matroid intersection variant of 𝒫-MOL under a covering constraint, whereas an EPTAS is known to exist under a budget constraint. This highlights a qualitative difference between these two types of linear constraints that does not arise in the single-matroid setting.

        Abstract
We study the following class of matroid optimization problems with a linear constraint (P-MOL).
Given a matroid M = (E, I), two nonnegative weight functions v, w : E → R≥0 , and a threshold
L ∈ R≥0 , find opt v(S) where S is either an independent set or a base of M satisfying a budget-type
constraint: w(S) ≤ L or w(S) ≥ L, and opt ∈ {min, max}. P-MOL provides a unified representation
for a broad family of NP-hard optimization problems, including budgeted matroid independent
set, constrained minimum-basis, and knapsack-cover variants with a matroid constraint.
Also, it naturally extends to multiple matroid constraints. In particular, we consider the matroid
intersection cover (MIC) problem, where feasibility is defined by the common independent sets
of two matroids and one seeks minimum v(S) subject to w(S) ≥ L.
    Our main result is a unified efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS) for all

a feasible solution S whose value is at most (1 + ε)OPT for minimization variants and at least

    1    Introduction
Matroids offer a unifying abstraction for “independence” in combinatorial structures: they
capture linear independence in vector spaces, forests in graphs, and many other systems
constrained by an exchange principle. A matroid is a set system (E, I), where E is a finite
set and I ⊆ 2E are the independent sets (IS) such that (i) ∅ ∈ I, (ii) for all A ∈ I and
B ⊆ A it holds that B ∈ I, and (iii) for all A, B ∈ I where |A| > |B|, there is e ∈ A \ B
such that B ∪ {e} ∈ I.1 A broad range of classical problems can be cast as matroid

1.2    Our Contribution
We present (in Section 2) a unified approximation framework for P-MOL problems by
generalizing a technique of Hassin and Levin [20]. This allows to obtain an EPTAS for all
non-trivial variants of P. Specifically, for every fixed ε > 0 there exists an algorithm which,
given an instance AP , outputs a feasible solution S satisfying

   opt = min =⇒ v(S) ≤ (1 + ε) OPTP ,           opt = max =⇒ v(S) ≥ (1 − ε) OPTP .

The running time is h(1/ε) · poly(|AP |) for an arbitrary function h. This resolves the
complexity status of all members of P-MOL, as none of these problems admits a fully
polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) [15]. Table 1 presents the best known
results for the P-MOL class. Results obtained in this paper are marked in boldface.
    We also consider the natural extension of P-MOL variants to matroid intersection. For
budgeted matroid intersection, an EPTAS was presented in [12]. In contrast to our
positive result for the P-MOL class, where matroid optimization is over a single matroid
constraint, we show that a unified EPTAS is unlikely to exist for all P-MOL variants,
already when the single matroid constraint is replaced by a matroid intersection constraint.
Specifically, we prove (in Section 3) that MIC does not admit an EPTAS unless W[1] = FPT.

1.3    Techniques
A Unified EPTAS for P-MOL
For Budgeted Matroid Independent Set, as well as for its extension to Budgeted
Matroid Intersection, recent works [13, 12] give EPTASs based on the representative-set
methodology. Roughly, it computes a small candidate pool that is guaranteed to contain the
high-value elements of some near-optimal solution, and then recovers the near-optimum by
exhaustive enumeration over this pool. However, this approach inherently (i) loses the profit
of O(1) elements, and (ii) may drop O(1) elements to restore feasibility. Thus, a solution
output by the representative set approach may be a non-basis for the given matroid. It may
also be infeasible w.r.t. a covering constraint. Therefore, the EPTASs of [13, 12] cannot
be extended to EPTASs for the entire P-MOL class, which must handle both IS(M) and
bases(M), and all four choices of (opt, ▷).
    Instead, we generalize (in Section 2) a technique of Hassin and Levin [20] to obtain a
unified EPTAS for all members of P-MOL under a general matroid constraint. The following
is a high-level overview of the algorithmic framework.
    Given a constant-factor guarantee V̂ for OPT, we bucket elements according to their
values ve . Elements with ve ≤ εV̂ are classified as small, while the remaining elements are
partitioned into O(1/ε2 ) narrow buckets. We note that any optimal solution contains only
O(1/ε) large elements. This allows us to enumerate configuration vectors ⃗k that specify the
number of selected elements from each bucket.
    For a fixed configuration ⃗k, we enforce these counts by intersecting the matroid with
a partition matroid, yielding a matroid-intersection family F⃗k . We then use a Lagrangian
relaxation of the linear constraint w(S) ▷ L and compute λ⃗⋆k , an optimal value of the
multiplier λ.

           The main technical challenge is to convert the Lagrangian optimum into a feasible solution.
       At λ⃗⋆k , the family O⃗k of Lagrangian-optimal sets is well connected: any two of its members
       can be transformed into one another via a sequence of exchanges, each replacing at most one
       element per bucket. We compute sets S − , S + ∈ O⃗k that respectively minimize and maximize
       the signed violation of w(S) ▷ L, and hence lie on opposite sides of feasibility. Traversing the
       one-per-bucket exchange path from S − to S + , we select the first feasible set S ⋆ .
           Because elements within each bucket have nearly identical v-values, each exchange affects
       the objective value by at most the total bucket spread – that is, the difference between the
       maximum and minimum v-value within a bucket. Consequently, the first feasible set S ⋆
       yields an objective value within an additive O(εOPT) of the Lagrangian bound. Taking the
       best such S ⋆ over all configurations yields an EPTAS.
           We note that some variants in our descriptor-based formulation are related by standard
       reductions. Nevertheless, we keep the unified formulation for completeness and to make
       the scope of the algorithm explicit, since such reductions may not always preserve the
       approximation guarantees in a straightforward way. In particular, budget-type and covering-
       type constraints require careful treatment: the existence of an EPTAS for the budget setting
       under a matroid intersection constraint [12] does not, by itself, imply an analogous result for
       the covering setting. Our hardness result in Theorem 13 highlights this distinction. Therefore,
       we present the argument directly for the descriptor class P = (opt, F, ▷).


       Hardness of MIC

       We establish a parameterized lower bound for matroid intersection cover (MIC). Via
       a reduction from k-Clique, we show that MIC admits no EPTAS unless W [1] = FPT
       (Theorem 13). The novelty of our result lies in the fact that this reduction rules out an
       EPTAS, whereas a similar construction of [15] is used only to exclude an FPTAS. Our result
       complements recent applications of related reductions to 3-matroid intersection [16].
       Together, our findings demonstrate that for matroid intersection, different linear constraints
       (cover versus budget) lead to markedly different algorithmic behavior, in contrast to the case
       of a single matroid.

1.4   Related Work
Knapsack and approximation schemes
The 0/1-Knapsack problem is a canonical benchmark for approximation schemes. Early
work already established a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme [24], and dynamic-
programming–based FPTASs and their implications have since been extensively studied [8].
More recent progress has focused on fine-grained analyses and improved time–approximation
tradeoffs [4, 9].


Matroid and matching constraints with a single budget
Adding a matroid or matching feasibility constraint to 0/1-Knapsack gives rise to the
well-studied problems of Budgeted Matching and Budgeted Matroid Intersection.
A PTAS for both variants was obtained by Berger et al. [1]. Subsequent work strengthened
these results to EPTAS guarantees: for Budgeted Matroid Independent Set [13], and
for Budgeted Matching and Budgeted Matroid Intersection via representative
sets [12].
    While an FPTAS is ruled out for general instances of Budgeted Matroid Independent
Set [15], FPTASs are known for several special cases, including Cardinality-Constrained
Knapsack [5], Multiple-Choice Knapsack [22], and laminar matroids [14, 27]. Additional
variants of the problem have also been studied, for example in [11, 10, 17].
    P-MOL problems have also been studied in the covering setting (as opposed to a budget
constraint), in conjunction with a matroid feasibility constraint. For Lower-Bounded
Minimum Independent Set, the best known result prior to this work was a PTAS, due
to [6]. For constrained minimum spanning tree, a PTAS was given in [26], followed by
an EPTAS in [20]. Furthermore, a multi-criteria FPTAS is known for this problem [21].


Multiple budgets
When multiple budget constraints are present, PTASs are known for variants with either
matroid intersection or matching constraints, using techniques such as dependent randomized
rounding [7] and structural properties of matroid polytopes [19]. On the other hand, even
seemingly simple extensions face strong complexity barriers: for example, the Multidimen-
sional Knapsack problem with just two budget constraints already rules out an EPTAS
under standard complexity assumptions [23].

 4     Discussion
In this paper, we present tight approximation results for a broad class of matroid optimization
problems with a linear constraint, along with a hardness result for MIC. Our unified EPTAS
for all P-MOL problems resolves the complexity status of this class, and the hardness of
MIC suggests that such a unified EPTAS is unlikely to extend to all P-MOL variants once
the single matroid constraint is replaced by a matroid intersection constraint.
    A natural direction for future work is to characterize the approximability landscape of
P-MOL variants under matroid intersection constraints. In particular, the existence of a
PTAS for MIC remains open.
    Finally, it would be interesting to identify settings in which stronger guarantees are
attainable. For instance, for graphic matroids and for linear matroids given by an explicit
representation, we obtain an EPTAS, while the existence of an FPTAS in these cases remains
open.
